02Why now

What arc42 is, and why it matters now

AI tools can generate code, but they can’t read your intent. Documentation that records goals, contracts and decisions is how you hand it over.

What it is

arc42 is a free, open template for documenting software and system architecture. Its twelve sections give each kind of architecture information a clear place: goals and constraints, context, building blocks, runtime behaviour, deployment, crosscutting concepts, decisions, quality scenarios, risks and a glossary.

It is a structure, not a method, and it doesn’t care about notation: Markdown, text-based diagrams or UML all work. It fits well as docs-as-code, kept in the repository and reviewed like source.

It is free to use, even commercially, with credit to its creators, Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka.

Why it matters now

Teams lose context. People leave, systems grow and decisions fade. A consistent structure makes the why findable.

AI tools only know what is written. Coding agents generate code quickly but guess at intent. Goals, contracts and recorded decisions are how you give it to them.

Specifying and checking are gaining value. As more code is generated, stating what good looks like and verifying the result become the scarcer skills.

03How it helps

Pick what you want to do

We show how arc42 gets you there, what you do in the workshop, and what you leave with.

Spend less on AICut wasted tokens

AI coding tools start every session knowing nothing about your project. Without a written map they read lots of files and guess, and you pay for every token. A short, accurate architecture note (what the parts are, what each promises, what you decided and why) gives them what the code can’t tell.

In the workshop. You write the short version: a strategy table, block descriptions, one contract and one decision record. Then you test it with a prompt template and a simple three-way experiment.

Be realistic. Shorter is better. A February 2026 ETH Zurich study reported that long, auto-generated context files lowered success and raised cost by over 20%, so the aim is short, human-written and specific. You test the effect on your own tasks.

Build at workBuild systems and integrations with fewer surprises

Most integration trouble hides at the edges: who talks to whom, in what format, and what happens when it fails. arc42 gives you a context view, interface contracts, failure scenarios and decision records, so colleagues and vendors work from the same picture.

In the workshop. You draw the context and Level-1 views, write a contract with error modes, and trace one runtime scenario with a failure branch.

Be realistic. It makes your design visible, so it can be questioned before it is expensive to change.

Start somethingTurn an idea into a brief anyone can build from

Founders and freelancers need to explain an idea to developers, clients and AI tools without it being misread. Quality goals, constraints such as budget, team and deadline, and a context view turn a vague idea into something others can build, price and challenge.

In the workshop. Use your own idea as the workshop case if you like. You leave with goals, constraints, a context view and a list of risks.

Be realistic. Use it to sharpen the idea before you test the market.

Ride the AI waveBuild the skills AI makes more valuable

As AI writes more of the code, the scarce skills move towards deciding structure, stating what good looks like, spotting AI’s mistakes and recording why. Those are the skills this workshop practises.

In the workshop. In the AI lab, AI drafts sections from your notes, then your team red-teams the result and decides what to keep.

Be realistic. You practise judging AI output, a skill that stays useful whatever tools change.

04The cost of not writing it down

What goes wrong without it

Knowledge lives in heads

Newcomers wait for someone to explain how things fit together.

Decisions get forgotten

Teams re-debate old choices, or break them by accident.

Qualities stay vague

“Fast” and “secure” mean different things to different people.

Machines read it too

AI tools act on what is written and guess what isn’t.

05Outcomes

What you will be able to do

Set the goals

Identify stakeholders and write quality goals with numbers instead of adjectives.

Draw the system

Sketch a context view and a Level-1 building-block view, then write one component contract.

Show behaviour

Describe a runtime scenario with a failure branch, and a deployment view.

Record why

Write an architecture decision record (ADR) that lists the road not taken.

Work with AI

Let AI draft a section, then find and fix its mistakes.

Write for agents

Shape documentation so both people and coding agents can use it.

06The programme

The day, hour by hour

Thirteen short parts. Each part has a finished example and then your turn. You build one document across the day: your own arc42 skeleton, section by section, for a real system your team knows.

  1. Morning: foundations to strategy

  2. 09:00

    Opening

    Why architecture goes undocumented, how we will learn, and the rules for using AI today. Form teams, choose your system and set up your tools, then take a short baseline quiz you will retake at the end.

    You leave with: a team, a case and a working arc42 file

  3. 09:30

    Foundations

    What architecture is, why it is a set of trade-offs, and what good documentation is not. Stakeholders and concerns, views, the C4 zoom levels, and the twelve arc42 sections. A quick Markdown and Mermaid warm-up.

    Warm-up exercise

  4. 10:05Break, 15 minutes
  5. 10:20

    Section 1: goals, quality and stakeholders

    Write a requirements overview that names no technology, then turn vague qualities like “fast” and “secure” into scenarios with numbers. Find the stakeholders and what each expects.

    Exercise 1 · one page, peer reviewed

  6. 11:10

    Section 2: constraints

    Sort constraints from decisions from requirements with the three-question test, then write your own numbered constraints.

    Exercise 2 · numbered constraints

  7. 11:25

    Section 3: context and scope

    Treat your system as a black box. Draw the business context, then record the technical channels in an interface table.

    Exercise 3 · context diagram and table

  8. 11:55

    Section 4: solution strategy

    Turn each quality goal into an approach, a reason and the trade-off you accept. A neighbour reads only your table and guesses your architecture.

    Exercise 4 · strategy table

  9. 12:15Lunch, 45 minutes

  10. Afternoon: structure, behaviour and decisions

  11. 13:00

    Section 5: building blocks

    Split the system into five to nine blocks, name their responsibilities and interfaces, then write a contract with pre-conditions, post-conditions, invariants and error modes for your riskiest block.

    Exercises 5a and 5b · Level-1 view and one contract

  12. 13:50

    Sections 6 to 8: runtime, deployment, crosscutting

    Draw one scenario as a sequence diagram with a failure branch, map every block to where it runs, and name the rules that recur across blocks.

    Exercises 6, 7 and 8

  13. 14:35Break, 15 minutes
  14. 14:50

    Section 9: decisions

    Write an architecture decision record with real alternatives and at least one real trade-off, so a new teammate understands why not the other option.

    Exercise 9 · one ADR

  15. 15:20

    Sections 10 to 12: quality, risks, glossary

    Grow your quality tree with a change scenario and a failure scenario, then list risks with mitigations and owners, and define your terms once.

    Exercises 10 and 11

  16. Late afternoon: AI and agents

  17. 15:40

    AI lab

    Have an assistant draft sections from your notes. Then red-team the result for ignored instructions, contradictions between sections and unsupported claims, and repair it, giving every AI line a verdict.

    Exercise 12 · red-teamed AI draft

  18. 16:20

    Agents as readers

    What humans and coding agents each need from documentation: short indexes, contracts, stable IDs and reasons. Turn an invariant into a test, and see how to check the effect on your own work.

  19. 16:35

    Close

    Check your skeleton against a checklist, walk the gallery, retake the quiz, rate your own progress and leave with a 30-day plan.

    You leave with: a complete first-draft arc42

12Designed from the evidence

Why the lab works the way it does

Every design choice in the lab traces to published research, cited below.

Producing beats rereading

A review of ten study techniques found that practice testing and distributed practice earned the highest utility ratings, while summarising, highlighting and rereading rated low. So each lesson ends with recall questions, reviews return at 1, 3, 7 and 21 days, and the lab has you write the document instead of reading about it.

Source 1

Draft first, then AI

In a 2025 PNAS study of nearly 1,000 high-school students, unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice grades by 48%, yet students scored 17% lower on the exam once it was removed. A version built with tutoring guardrails largely mitigated the harm. In the lab you write your own sections before any AI sees them, and when you red-team a draft with AI you record each suggestion as accepted, rejected or edited, with a reason.

Source 2

Design beats a chatbot

In a 2025 Harvard randomised trial (194 students analysed), a carefully designed AI tutor taught physics better than an active-learning class, in a median 49 minutes against an assumed 60. It was built on research-based teaching principles. We use the same principles without handing your thinking to a machine: one step at a time, a worked example to compare with, and immediate checks on your own work.

Source 3

Support that can fade

Guidance that helps beginners can get in the way of experts, a finding known as the expertise reversal effect. So the worked example is optional, and every lab step has an “Experienced?” version that asks more of you.

Source 4

Testing yourself beats rereading

A 2017 meta-analysis of 118 articles (15,427 participants) found practice testing beat restudying by g = 0.51, and beat doing nothing by g = 0.93. The largest effects came when the final test followed practice by one to six days. So every lesson ends with questions you answer before you see the answer, and missed cards return after a day.

Source 5

Explaining your reasons

A 2018 meta-analysis of 69 effect sizes found that prompting learners to explain to themselves improved learning, with a mean effect of g = 0.55. In the lab each decision and each AI suggestion you keep or reject carries a short reason in your own words, which is that kind of prompt.

Source 6

Why lessons are short and resumable

Across HarvardX and MITx courses, 15.4% of learners who intended to complete did so in 2017-18, and 3.1% of all registrants. Completion among those who paid for a verified track was 46%. The authors point to human support as what matters most. So lessons are short, the course remembers your place, and the first two are free to try.

Source 7

A mirror, not a rule

In a preregistered experiment (704 adults, August 2026), a short message after each exercise describing how people had used an AI assistant cut how often they asked it for complete answers (odds ratio 0.47) and left their unaided results somewhat higher. The message only described their behaviour; it did not tell them what to do. The lab's process mirror does the same for your document: how much you typed, pasted and inserted from templates.

Source 8

The studies cited here are peer-reviewed and mostly involve students. Effect sizes vary by setting, so we use them as design principles. Each source is linked so you can read the original.

  1. Dunlosky et al. (2013), Psychological Science in the Public Interest, summarised by the Association for Psychological Science
  2. Bastani et al. (2025), Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26)
  3. Kestin et al. (2025), Scientific Reports 15, 17458
  4. Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller (2003), The expertise reversal effect, Educational Psychologist 38(1)
  5. Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan (2017), Rethinking the use of tests: a meta-analysis of practice testing, Review of Educational Research 87(3)
  6. Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi and Winne (2018), Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis, Educational Psychology Review 30
  7. Reich and Ruipérez-Valiente (2019), The MOOC pivot, Science 363(6423)
  8. Maier, Schwabe, Schneider and Feuerriegel (2026), Designing Against Deskilling: metacognitive feedback reduces cognitive offloading to LLM assistants, arXiv:2609.20143 (preprint)

13Audience

Who it’s for

New to architecture documentation. Every section starts with a finished example and early exercises are mostly filled in. If you can explain how an app works, you can follow along. No UML needed.

Senior engineers, tech leads and architects. Go beyond the template: write quality scenarios with measurable response targets, interface contracts with invariants and error modes, and decision records that capture the road not taken. Then make the result useful to coding agents and keep it from drifting.

Analysts, testers, managers and founders who need one shared picture between the business and the build.

Already fluent in arc42? Expect a quick pass through the template, with the depth in contracts, quality scenarios, the AI lab and agent-readable documentation.

15Questions

Questions

What is arc42?

A free, open template with twelve sections for writing down how a software system is built and why. It was created by Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka.

Is this the official arc42 training?

It is an independent workshop built on the free arc42 template, and it is not affiliated with or endorsed by arc42. It does not lead to a certification.

I’m an experienced engineer. What’s in it for me?

The template is the easy part. The depth is in measurable quality scenarios, contracts with invariants and error modes, decision records with real alternatives, an AI lab where you red-team generated documentation, and designing docs that coding agents can use without drifting.

I’m new to this. Will I keep up?

Yes. Every section starts with a finished example, early exercises are mostly filled in, and you work in a team. The support fades as you gain confidence.

Will this really cut my AI costs?

Short, specific documentation gives coding tools the context they need without reading the whole repository. The workshop shows you how to measure the effect on your own work.

Where and when?

Saturday 30 January 2027, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm at UWI St Augustine. Registered participants get the exact room by email before the day.

Do I need to know UML?

No. Boxes, arrows and plain words are enough.

Which system do we document?

One your team can explain from memory, such as a school library, a clinic booking system or a maxi-taxi tracker. Please don’t share confidential details.

Will we use AI?

Yes, but you write the first draft yourselves. Then you use AI to find gaps, and you check every line it produces.

What should I bring?

A laptop with a Markdown editor that previews Mermaid diagrams, or a shared document your team can edit.

Is it a certification?

No. It is a practical workshop that ends with a document you can use.

This workshop is independent. It is built on the free arc42 template, which was created by Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka, and is not affiliated with or endorsed by arc42. It does not lead to a certification.

Sources and how we use them

arc42: docs.arc42.org. On context files for AI coding agents: a February 2026 ETH Zurich study (Gloaguen et al.) reported that long, LLM-generated context files lowered task success and raised inference cost by over 20%, as summarised by Little Bear Apps. Other analyses report benefits from concise, human-written files. Findings are early and vary by tool and task, so we teach you to test on your own work.
